query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, pre-engineered hafnium-based surface coating to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a self-healing HfO2 protective layer.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., VZrHfNbTa) that experiences rapid oxidation and associated degradation (weight gain, scale spallation, and loss of mechanical integrity) at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (on the order of 100–120 μm) hafnium-based reactive coating onto the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at approximately 1300°C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air or pure oxygen) for durations on the order of 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The pre-engineered hafnium coating transforms into a dense, adherent HfO2 scale that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the hafnium coating rapidly oxidizes to form a self-healing HfO2 layer that reduces further oxidation of the underlying alloy. This protective layer minimizes weight gain and structural degradation compared to the untreated condition.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hafnium-coated alloy will show significantly lower weight gain and a thinner, more uniform oxide scale relative to the uncoated alloy after exposure under the specified conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically develop severe oxidation, high weight gain, and microstructural degradation (e.g., observed dents, oxidation, and pulverization) under extreme temperature oxidizing environments.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under continuous high-temperature exposure (around 1300°C) in oxidizing atmospheres; deviations in temperature significantly lower or thermal cycling conditions may affect the formation or stability of the HfO2 layer.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adherence of the HfO2 scale under cyclic thermal stresses and its potential impact on the bulk mechanical integrity of the alloy require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same refractory high-entropy alloy; one set will be coated with a 100–120 μm hafnium layer, and the other will be left uncoated. Expose both sets simultaneously in an air or oxygen atmosphere at 1300°C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, measure weight gain per unit area, oxide scale thickness, and perform microstructural analyses using SEM and XRD to assess the oxide layer’s density and continuity.
measurements: Microstructural integrity and adhesion of the oxide scale (via SEM analysis)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hafnium-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than approximately 40% reduction in weight gain) and formation of a dense, continuous HfO2 layer compared to the uncoated samples under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Ultra-high Temperature Oxidation-Resistant Alloys (UTORAs) have received a lot of attention due to the increased research demand for deep space exploration around the world. However, UTORAs have the disadvantages of easy oxidation and chalking. So, in this study, a UTORAs is prepared by hot-press sintering on VZrHfNbTa (HEA: High Entropy Alloys can generally be defined as more than five elements by the equal atomic ratio or close to the equal atomic ratio alloying, the mixing entropy is higher than the melting entropy of the alloy, generally forming a high entropy solid solution phase of a class of alloys.) a substrate coated with hafnium. The bonding mechanism, resistance to high-temperature oxidation, and hardness of the sample tests are carried out. The results show that zirconium in the matrix will diffuse into the hafnium coating during the high-temperature sintering process and form the HfZr alloy transition layer, the coating thickness of the composite is about 120 μm, and the diffusion distance of zirconium in the hafnium coating is about 60 μm, this transition layer chemically combines the hafnium coating and the HEA substrate into a monolithic alloy composite. The results

The weight gain of the coated sample after oxidation is 56.56 mg/cm2, which is only 57.7% compared to the weight gain of the uncoated sample (98.09 mg/cm2 for uncoated), and the surface of the uncoated HEA shows obvious dents, oxidation, and pulverization occurred on the surface and interior of the sample. In contrast, the coated composite alloy sample mainly undergoes surface oxidation sintering to form a dense HfO2 protective layer, and the internal oxidation of the hafnium-coated VZrHfNbTa composite alloy is significantly lower than that of the uncoated VZrHfNbTa HEA.

High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. decision.trend: Initial studies on refractory HEAs primarily characterized the baseline oxidation behavior and mechanical performance. In 2019, researchers showed that incorporating chromium (along with tantalum) promoted formation of a CrTaO4‐based oxide that acted as a protective layer during long-duration high-temperature exposure. Later work (2023) further demonstrated that adding Cr in laser-cladded coatings refines the microstructure and enhances both hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance. Most recently, a study using a hafnium coating on a HEA substrate (2023) indicated that an engineered surface layer can chemically bond with the alloy and form a protective oxide, lowering weight gain during oxidation at ultra‐high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, a single, straightforward intervention that reliably forms a dense, protective oxide scale—without additional, multi‐component alloying or adverse effects on mechanical integrity—remains undemonstrated. The challenge is to improve oxygen resistance under extreme-temperature oxidizing conditions using one targeted modification that does not compromise the bulk structural properties.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, pre-engineered reactive element coating (e.g., a hafnium-based layer) designed to form a self-healing HfO2 scale during high-temperature exposure
decision.why: Surface modification via a hafnium coating leverages the trend where reactive elements (such as Cr or Hf) promote the in-situ formation of protective oxide scales. The hafnium layer is expected to transform at service conditions (1200–1400°C in an oxidizing atmosphere) into a dense, slowly growing HfO2 film that retards oxygen ingress. This approach follows from prior evidence that coatings (as in the Hf-coated HEA study) markedly reduce oxidation weight gain. A falsification experiment could involve exposing both coated and uncoated samples to 1300°C in air or pure oxygen for 100 hours and then comparing oxide scale thickness, weight gain, and microstructural integrity. A lack of significant improvement in oxidation resistance in the coated sample would falsify the hypothesis.
